cells.tense: You are here, present with the pen, sensing what is growing and giving it room.
cells.ask: Name one thing you are tending and tell one person why it matters to you today.
cells.core:
You are with it right now, not ahead of it and not behind. What is coming you can feel without grabbing at it, and that makes you good at tending things that are still small. You give a thing the time it needs to take its own shape, and the pace is the point.

The ones in front of you get your actual attention, not a schedule. When something you care about starts to move, you move with it instead of announcing it. That steadiness costs you the noise of drama, and it is worth it. If this balance is going to feed something next, feed it slowly: one more thing you really care about, given the same quiet attention you already give the ones here.

cells.tense: You are already bracing for a future that has not happened yet, and it is shaping what you do now.
cells.ask: Wait one full day before acting on a growing thing, and tell no one what you saw until the day is up.
cells.core:
You are ahead of it. You can see the next move and the one after, so you are already living there, minding a version of this that has not arrived. That is not care done wrong. It is care that ran ahead of what is actually here. From where you sit it feels like being ready. From the outside it can look like hovering.

So your hands are busy with a future while the thing in front of you is still trying to take its first shape. You are watching for problems it does not have yet, and that is tiring. Some of it lands as pressure rather than support. Letting the future stay unwritten for a while is what brings this back. Hold one thing loosely for a day before you reach for it.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that has already closed behind you, waiting for it to open.
cells.ask: Tell one person one thing you want to grow, then ask them one question about what they see.
cells.core:
The sensing is not gone. You just stopped bringing it in. What is growing gets followed from a distance, with your care kept out of the room, and you have been quiet for a while now. It is not that you have nothing to tend. It is that you have not turned toward the living thing in front of you.

What is missing is not feeling. It is letting what you want be seen while it is still small. Do not push warmth into a cold room; go the other way. Listen to someone, ask what they notice, and let their answer land before you decide what to do with it. That is what pulls the current back. Register one want out loud this week.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped tending it out loud, and that is the part you can start again.

cells.tense: You are already writing in a room you keep describing as vacant, pen down but still in motion.
cells.ask: Pick one small growing thing you already do and say out loud that you are the one tending it.
cells.core:
You are already shaping what is around you, and you describe it as something that happens on its own. You notice what is tender before anyone names it. You adjust your pace, your tone, your timing. People feel that, and it changes how they grow near you. None of it is an accident, and you keep filing it under how things are.

Your attention is the thing doing the growing, and you leave your name off it. When this balance is back, you are not only present to what grows, you know the work is yours. Go to the simpler form of the same line: pick one small practice and do it plainly, then admit you chose it.
cells.sheetLine: You are already tending it, so say so and stop calling it nothing.

attempts.check: The record supports the mechanism directing energy into the partner's action rather than pushing the seat directly, but each cell turns that mechanism into a specific inner intention, which a reader could rightly say is not in the record. The asks survive being wrong because they are one concrete act toward the seat or the partner's action, not a feeling, and they do not promise an outcome. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is the crisp diagnostic line in each core, which makes the tension sound more settled than it may be; each draft trims it to a plain observation a person could answer back to. The four cores stay life-level, using the same verb and place at every status, and Too Much and Too Little read as opposite failures: pouring imagined needs ahead of time versus guarding a shut door behind it.
